doc.title: Dawoud Sabu Adeyola interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 30, 2025

title: What listeners should get, anger in the music, Dexter Gordon's Army story
summary: Coltrane's answer, free jazz as rage not anger, Dexter in the Army, and the state of the country.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Life philosophy: faith, karma and how to live

blocks.x: Yes. And it made me wonder what you hope listeners get from your music? I don’t know if I could have phrased that in a better way, but do you hope — I think you know what I mean.

Yeah. I think my answer would be similar to what John Coltrane was asked a similar question one time and I loved his answer. He said, “I hope to make people realize that we live in a big beautiful universe. We are only a tiny part of a beautiful universe and that I will hope that my listeners realize that there is meaning to life. Life has meaning and certainly life does have meaning, and that this meaning can be expressed through music. And something like that he said. And I always thought that that was really the short but very appropriate answer, that music is a reflection of life, and life has a very deep meaning and we should never take it for granted. And that the musician, especially the spiritually attuned musician is always trying to connect. You know? Like Albert Ayler said, music is the healing force of the universe. I love that quote from him too. And that the musicians that I love the most are the ones that are not afraid, you know, to stretch the boundaries and even break the rules. Like I tell students all the time, you have to learn the rules so you know how to break them.

That’s a good one. I’ve heard people say and write about free jazz, because you mentioned Albert Ayler — a lot of times it seems like why are these musicians so angry. And I once asked Rashied Ali about that and he said it was more about just a reflection of the times. I wonder if you have a thought about that?

Yeah I think anger is a misinterpretation. Like one time they asked Archie Shepp was he angry. This was back in the heyday when Archie was pretty big in the ‘60s. And he said, he said, “Why are musicians so — are you guys angry?” He said, “No we’re not angry, we’re enraged.” You know? We’re enraged about the conditions, about the history, about the way we’ve been treated, about — Dexter Gordon talks about, in his biography he talks about how when he was in the Army, right — a Lieutenant or maybe a Sergeant or a superior officer came in to his space, right? And he had a picture of his wife there on the dresser, by the bed. And the guy said something — he didn’t say exactly what he said, but he said something disrespectful, because the wife was lighter skinned and very beautiful. And he asked him who is that. He said, “That’s my wife.” And he said something that Dexter didn’t like and so he decked him.
He decked him. He hit him.

He hit him, punched him out. And you know Dexter’s about 6 feet 7, you know a big guy. Anyway so he hit this guy because he said something about his wife or her complexion or something like what are you doing with a white woman. Something like

that. And so he hit the guy and then he went on to jail, to the brig or what they call it in the Army you know. And then he stayed there — he had a bad, like Lester Young, he had a bad military experience you know. They said Lester was never the same after he came out of the Army. And you could hear it in the records the way he was playing with Count Basie and whatnot, before he got drafted and — his records afterwards they were still good but they weren’t on the same level. But Dexter went through that and what he said in terms of anger he said that it seems to him that America should be grateful, especially to the bebop musicians, most of whom were veterans — as he said, it seems like the veterans of World War II are actually the ones who created bebop you know. And a lot of them were vets, including Al Tinney, Dexter, Elvin Jones, a lot of times they didn’t make a big deal about it. You might not have known it, you know, but they actually went and put their lives on the line for this country and then to come back and be treated in such a way, it’s upsetting. It’s upsetting. But when it comes to artists I think more so than anger it’s about expressing the desire or a need or a real, you know, a real belief that things can be better. That we can be better but we all have to do something. You know we can’t just sit back and just tsk tsk, and just say oh too bad. But we have to all be active participants in trying to make things better. And so like a lot of people were upset when John Coltrane kind of went into outer space towards the end you know, breaking the rules and playing against tradition and playing different. Even Miles, even Miles did it a different way, but I think all of the artists they were trying to say to us that you know we can’t be stagnant. We can’t be complacent. That we have to keep moving the boundaries. We have to keep expanding our horizons. That’s our job as artists you know. If we’re not doing that — and most of the artists, even European artists like Picasso and Michelangelo — all great artists, they were all involved in trying to expand the boundaries, you know, and get people to see things in another way, hopefully a better way.
Well said. And all the more important in these particular times.

Absolutely. Yeah. We’re seeing a retrogression now you know. You see a lot of people now talking about — just throwing up their hands and moving to another country. Because things are that bad. I mean you’ve got people trying to re-make this whole democratic experience you know, in their own image, which is not progressive, it’s digressive. You know? And it seems like they want to go back to a time in history which, you know, most Americans are embarrassed about. You know, most Americans are wishing we never had slavery. Wishing that we never had, that it didn’t take centuries for women to be able to get to vote, you know, and that they shouldn’t — most of us if we could go back and re-write history we’d try to write in the true image of what the democratic ideal says it’s supposed to be, which is freedom, justice and equality for all — equal opportunities — and we know that that has not been the case.
